about: Part of the reference catalogue: designs from Núñez Ares, Schoen and Goos (2023), the paper that introduces mixed-level OMARS designs (three-level quantitative and two-level categorical factors).

designs: the three example designs the paper prints (Designs 1-3: 24, 48 and 40 runs), with their runs in coded units, the features of Table 1, and the correlations and projection properties the text states; the 14-factor 48-run strength-3 array Design 2 starts from (its two-level columns); the zero counts of definitive screening designs the paper uses to explain why they cannot take several two-level factors; and the counts of the paper's computational search (Table 2).

There is no experiment with responses in the paper. Correlations are checked with evaluate_design on the printed matrices; the run and factor counts and the array's strength are checked too; zero counts, projection estimability and the search counts are manual, with what a script found where it could look.
Read with process_improve.experiments.reference_catalogue.reference_designs; tests/test_reference_catalogue.py recomputes every number that has a check.

source.title: Orthogonal Minimally Aliased Response Surface Designs for Three-Level Quantitative Factors and Two-Level Categorical Factors
source.publisher: Institute of Statistical Science, Academia Sinica
source.cite: Núñez Ares, Schoen and Goos (2023), "Orthogonal Minimally Aliased Response Surface Designs for Three-Level Quantitative Factors and Two-Level Categorical Factors", Statistica Sinica 33(1), 107-126
source.read: 2026-10-13, the accepted author version of the article (Statistica Sinica preprint SS-2020-0347, accepted subject to English editing, 30 pages); every number with its page and a short quotation. That version prints no page numbers, so each page is the page's place in it; the journal's pages 107-126 are from its online index.
source.rights: The article is protected by copyright and is not reproduced here; read it through its DOI. This file holds facts it reports (numbers, design matrices, data) and short quotations that locate each one, for citation and for checking software. The MIT licence of process-improve does not extend to them.

designs.notes: The captured runs satisfy every property the paper states (checked in a script): column sums 0, main effects mutually orthogonal and orthogonal to every quadratic and two-factor interaction column, every product of three columns sums to 0, the two-level part is a strength-3 array, and the 24 runs are a foldover (each run's negative is a run). Correlations are computed with the two-level factors as -1/+1 numeric columns, as the paper codes them (Section 2.1), and with the pure quadratics of the quantitative factors only.

expected.analysis: the average absolute correlation between the columns of all second-order effects (the 28 two-factor interactions of the eight factors and the four quadratic effects)

where.quote: the average absolute correlation between the columns corresponding to all second-order effects equals 0.15

check.disagreement: found 0.1739 over all 32 second-order columns (496 pairs). The correlations are those of the centred columns; the maximum quadratic correlation of 0.2 printed alongside reproduces with the same definition. Leaving out the six interactions of two categorical factors gives 0.1503, which would print as 0.15, but the paper says all second-order effects; with the quadratic columns not centred the full set gives 0.1564. Design 2's average (0.138) does not reproduce under either definition, so the paper's exact definition is unclear.

check.disagreement: found 0.1358 (absolute correlations of the centred columns over all 176 second-order columns); without the quadratics 0.1360, with uncentred quadratics 0.1339, and without the interactions of two categorical factors 0.1576. not_captured: Lemmas 1-3, Propositions 1-2 and Corollaries 1-3 (Section 2.2, PDF pp. 8-11): general necessary conditions with proofs, not numbers about a design. The three designs satisfy them: n - nIE0, n - nME0 and nIE0 - nME0 are multiples of four for every column of Table 1, as Section 4 says.
Equations (3.3)-(3.10), the integer program (PDF p. 14): a statement of method.
Section 3.1 (PDF p. 12): the earlier catalogue's 'up to six center points' and 'seven different OMARS designs' per basic design, which describe Nunez-Ares and Goos (2020), not this paper's designs.
Section 4.1 (PDF p. 19): 'when the total number of factors is greater than ten' the construction from scratch is expensive, a remark on computing time.

Figure 1a and 1b (PDF p. 26): which (n, m1 + m2) and (m1, m2) combinations gave a design, a scatter of symbols read off a figure; the 587 designs themselves are in the authors' repository (github.com/jnares/mixed-omars-designs-article), not in the article.

Restatements, captured once: the text's 1314, 1173, 973, 245, 123, 219, 488, 894 and 572 (PDF pp. 24-25) repeat Table 2; 'five three-level factors', 'four or more two-level categorical factors' and 'a multiple of eight' (PDF pp. 17, 19) repeat Table 1.
The statements that Designs 1, 2 and 3 are foldover designs (PDF pp. 18, 19, 21): properties, not numbers; each is confirmed in the design's notes.
